title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
keyIdea: The best rectangle using bar k at full height stretches left and right until the first shorter bar on each side. A rising monotonic stack finds both: when a shorter bar i arrives, the popped bar's right limit is i − 1 and its left limit is just after the new stack top. Each bar is pushed and popped once.

approaches.name: Brute force: every range
approaches.idea: For every start i, extend j to the right keeping the minimum height; area = min × width.
approaches.why: n²/2 ranges, O(1) each with a running minimum. ~5·10⁹ at n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Previous + next smaller (two passes)
approaches.idea: For each bar find the index of the previous smaller bar and the next smaller bar with monotonic stacks; width = next − prev − 1, area = height × width.
approaches.why: Two stack passes plus one loop, each O(n). Needs two extra arrays of size n.

approaches.name: One-pass monotonic stack
approaches.idea: Keep indices with rising heights. When heights[i] is shorter than the top, pop and measure: height × (i − 1 − new top), or × i if the stack is empty. Finally pop the rest with i = n.
approaches.why: Every index is pushed once and popped once, and each pop does O(1) work.

quiz.q: When a bar is popped because heights[i] is shorter, where does its rectangle end on the right?
options: At i − 1: bar i is the first shorter bar to its right
At the end of the array

quiz.q: After popping, the stack is empty. What's the width?
options: i: nothing on the left is shorter, so it spans 0 … i − 1

quiz.q: Why is there a final loop with i = heights.size()?
options: Bars still on the stack never met a shorter bar, so they stretch to the right edge
